overview: The Community Development Board is a municipal body in Medford that conducts site plan reviews, subdivision approvals, and recommends zoning ordinance amendments to the City Council. Since November 2024, the board has been engaged in a comprehensive citywide rezoning initiative to align local regulations with the 2023 Comprehensive Plan. This effort involves establishing new sub-districts for major commercial corridors, such as Mystic Avenue, Salem Street, and Boston Avenue, while modernizing residential standards for accessory dwelling units. As of October 2026, the board has shifted toward finishing a 'cleanup' of the zoning ordinance and preparing for new phases of rezoning for the Tufts University campus and the Wellington district.

threads.name: Medford and West Medford Squares Rezoning
threads.summary: The board began public information sessions for Medford Square and West Medford Square in May 2025, proposing increased density and height transitions near Interstate 93. Throughout 2026, the board held a series of special joint meetings with the City Council to refine district boundaries, parking mandates, and historic preservation incentives. Following substantial public feedback regarding commercial focus and residential context, the board closed its public hearings and recommended approval of the new mixed-use districts in March 2026. The process also included the creation of a City Hall Overlay District to facilitate a large-scale redevelopment project known as Transom.

threads.name: Boston Avenue Neighborhood Corridor District
threads.summary: The board introduced draft zoning concepts for the Boston Avenue corridor in mid-2025 and entered formal joint hearings with the City Council in May 2026. Deliberations focused on sub-district height limits, shadow impacts, and the regulation of private student housing. The board reached a consensus on building heights and operational standards for 'purpose-built student housing' before forwarding a final recommendation to the City Council in September 2026. Despite its recommendation, the board later expressed disappointment regarding subsequent changes made to the district by the City Council prior to ordainment.

threads.name: Residential District and ADU Zoning Reform
threads.summary: The board initiated a major overhaul of neighborhood and urban residential zoning in early 2025, proposing five new districts to replace existing residential codes. A significant portion of this work involved aligning local rules with state law regarding Accessory Dwelling Units (ADUs), including the removal of owner-occupancy and parking requirements in certain areas. Public testimony was deeply divided between residents seeking more housing density and those concerned about infrastructure capacity and neighborhood character. In late 2025, the board voted to continue these hearings to late 2026 to allow for more density analysis and to coordinate with the City Council's spring legislative calendar.

threads.name: Tufts University Institutional Zoning
threads.summary: In May 2025, the board began investigating the creation of a dedicated institutional zoning district for the Tufts University campus to address gaps in municipal oversight. Because the university is protected under the state's Dover Amendment, the board sought a model that enforces reasonable dimensional standards like building heights and setbacks to protect abutting residential areas. While initial joint discussions with the City Council occurred in 2026, the board determined the process should not be rushed. Formal drafting and consultant procurement for this phase were scheduled to resume in late 2026.

threads.name: Development Incentives and Ecological Standards
threads.summary: To improve development quality, the board recommended the Green Score Zoning Amendment in early 2025, establishing an ecological performance system for new projects. The board also worked to reform citywide development incentives that grant additional height or density in exchange for public benefits. By mid-2026, members identified 'technical flaws' in incentive tables that failed to produce affordable housing in smaller projects, leading to a proposed overhaul of the bonus framework. This included shifting to multiplier-based calculations and refining definitions for community amenities like pocket parks.

threads.name: Major Site Plan Reviews
threads.summary: The board processed several large-scale development applications, most notably a 677-bed Tufts University dormitory at 401 Boston Avenue, which it approved with conditions for community transparency after months of review. Other major projects included the approval of a 34-room domestic violence shelter on St. Clair Road and ongoing hearings for a 248-unit multifamily development at 10 and 20 Revere Beach Parkway. The board frequently utilized the site plan review process to mandate conditions such as construction management plans, tree replacement, and shuttle service requirements to mitigate neighborhood impacts.

threads.name: Salem Street Corridor Rezoning
threads.summary: The board held public hearings in early 2025 to establish the Salem Street Corridor District, which proposed mixed-use sub-districts and incentive zoning options. Following feedback regarding traffic and building height near elementary schools, the board recommended the amendments to the City Council in March 2025 with modifications to residential alignments. In late 2025, the board approved an additional amendment to return specific nodes on Salem Street and Park Street to the Mixed Use 1 district as originally intended.
